transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, um... I guess I'm here because I just can't function properly at work anymore. I teach high school, and we have to record these lesson videos for the portal. And when I watch them back, I just can't stop seeing this... this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face. It's awful. And once I notice it, I just know that the students, the parents, the other staff... they must all be staring right at it instead of listening to a single word I'm actually teaching. 

Which is incredibly frustrating because I put a lot of work into those lessons. Actually, the parents have been so demanding this term anyway. I had this one mom email me at 11 PM on a Sunday asking about the grading rubric for the midterm essays. I mean, I posted that rubric on the class page three weeks ago. I spend hours formatting those documents because the district's software is from, like, 2010 and it completely messes up the text alignment if you don't code it perfectly. It's a total nightmare trying to get IT to fix anything, too. 

But... yeah. The videos. I just feel like everyone is just staring at my face and how swollen it is.
Is it always this particular side of your face that you notice looking swollen, or does it vary?

Yeah, it's... it's always the exact same side. Like I was saying, it's always that one crooked, swollen-looking part of my face on those videos. I just can't stop seeing it. And I know, I just *know* the students and parents aren't listening to a single word of the lesson, they're just staring right at it. 

Which... you know, I actually tried to fix how it looked by buying a new HD webcam and one of those ring lights? Out of my own pocket, of course. The district won't reimburse us for any tech upgrades. My department head, Susan, she told me to just use the natural light from the window. But my classroom window faces the staff parking lot, and there's this massive oak tree that blocks the sun anyway. Not to mention the maintenance guys are always out there running the leaf blowers right during my prep period when I'm trying to record. It's incredibly loud, you can't hear anything over those gas motors. They really should switch to electric ones, it's so much better for the environment and the noise pollution is just ridiculous. I brought it up at the last union meeting, but nobody really seemed to care. 

But, um... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, the swelling. Yeah, it doesn't vary. It's always that same side.
Is there anything else about your appearance that you're concerned about, or is it just this one side of your face?

No, no, it's really just... just that one side of my face. I don't really worry about the rest of me, like my body or my clothes or anything. 

I always make sure I dress professionally. I actually just had to buy a new iron, though, because my old one started leaking this weird rusty water all over my good dress shirts. It completely ruined this nice blue button-down my sister got me. I tried taking it to the dry cleaners on 4th street—you know, the one next to that bakery?—but the guy there said the stain was already set. Which is a huge shame because it's so hard to find clothes that fit right off the rack, and good tailors are just impossible to find now. My grandfather used to go to this guy downtown who measured everything by hand, but that whole block got bought out by developers last year. They're turning it into these luxury condos that nobody in this town can even afford, especially not on a teacher's salary. It's ridiculous how much rent has gone up around here, honestly. I was looking at my lease renewal the other day and they want to raise it by twelve percent. Twelve! 

But... wait, I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. Right, no, just my face. Nothing else.
Do you think that other people actually notice this swelling on your face when they see you in person, or is it something you're more aware of when you watch the videos?

Well, I... I definitely think they notice it in person, too. Like, I can feel them looking at it when I'm standing at the front of the classroom. It's just... the videos are where *I* have to see it, you know? But in person, I know they see it. 

Actually, the other day in the teachers' lounge, I was talking to Mark—he teaches AP History—and I swear he kept looking right at that side of my face. Which is so distracting, because we were trying to coordinate this cross-curricular project on the Industrial Revolution. It's such a great unit, we have the kids look at primary sources from textile mills. But getting the kids to actually read primary sources is like pulling teeth these days. They just want to look up a summary on their phones. I caught three kids using AI to write their essays last week. It's so obvious when they do it, too, because the vocabulary is completely wrong for a sophomore, and they never cite the textbook. The administration wants us to have this whole restorative justice circle about academic integrity instead of just giving them zeros. I mean, I'm all for understanding where the kids are coming from, but at some point, there have to be actual consequences, right? Otherwise, they're just going to go to college and fail out immediately because they don't know how to do the work. 

But, um... yeah, I'm pretty sure everyone notices it all the time, in person and on the videos. It's impossible to miss.
Have you ever seen a doctor or a dentist about the swelling on your face?

Well, I... no, I haven't actually gone to a doctor or a dentist about it. I mean, I thought about it, but... I don't know, I just haven't. 

I did try to make a dentist appointment a few months ago, just for a regular cleaning, you know? But my regular dentist, Dr. Evans, he retired. Just completely out of the blue. He sent out this letter saying he was moving to Florida to be closer to his grandkids, which, good for him, I guess, but he sold the practice to this huge corporate dental chain. And let me tell you, it is completely different now. They have all these TVs on the ceiling while they work on you, playing daytime talk shows, and the hygienists are always trying to upsell you on whitening treatments or electric toothbrushes. It feels more like a car dealership than a medical office. And they stopped taking my insurance! The district switched our provider last year to save money, and the new network is just terrible. You can't find anyone who takes it within a twenty-mile radius. I had to spend three hours on hold with the insurance company just to get a list of in-network providers, and half the numbers on the list were disconnected. It's so frustrating how broken the healthcare system is, especially for educators. We put in all these hours, and we can't even get decent dental coverage. 

So, yeah... no, I haven't had a professional look at the swelling. I just haven't had the time or the energy to deal with finding a new doctor who actually takes my insurance.
Has your concern about the appearance of your face affected your relationships with colleagues or students outside of the classroom?

Well, I... yeah, it definitely has. I mean, outside the classroom, it's... it's gotten pretty bad. I've completely fallen behind on my lesson planning, and I haven't been keeping up with my mentoring duties. I even had to step back from coaching the JV basketball team because I just... I can't get my work finished on time anymore. I'm spending so much time worrying about how I look, I just sit there at my desk. 

And the administration is definitely noticing. Principal Higgins has started documenting all my missed deadlines and the times I haven't been there to cover my duty periods. Which is so typical of Higgins, honestly. He's a micromanager. Ever since he took over last year, the whole school climate has just tanked. He instituted this new policy where we have to submit our lesson plans two weeks in advance on this clunky online portal that crashes every Friday afternoon. It's supposed to increase "transparency," but really it just means the district office can spy on what we're doing. And he's obsessed with the dress code, but only for the teachers! The kids are walking around in pajama pants and crop tops, and he doesn't say a word, but if a teacher wears jeans on a Thursday, he sends an email CCing the superintendent. It's just a completely toxic work environment. My friend Sarah, who teaches biology down the hall, she's already looking for jobs in the neighboring district because they actually have a strong union there. Ours just rolled over during the last contract negotiations, and we ended up with a pay freeze. 

But... anyway, yeah. Higgins is documenting everything, and I'm genuinely terrified I'm close to losing my position. It's just... it's taking over everything.
Do you feel like your concern about the appearance of your face is interfering with your ability to enjoy things you used to enjoy?

Well, I... I guess so. I mean, I don't really know if it's stopping me from enjoying things, because I don't even have time to do anything fun anymore anyway. Between the swelling and just... everything else. 

I used to love going to this trivia night on Thursdays at the pub downtown with some of the other teachers. It was our way to decompress, you know? But the pub changed ownership a few months ago, and they completely ruined the menu. They got rid of these amazing sweet potato fries they used to have and replaced them with this weird truffle oil stuff that just tastes like chemicals. And they raised the prices on all the craft beers. It's ridiculous. The whole downtown area is getting so gentrified. They tore down that old historic movie theater just to build another luxury apartment complex that nobody who actually works in this town can afford to live in. The traffic is a nightmare now, too, because they haven't updated the infrastructure to handle all the new residents. It takes me an extra twenty minutes just to get through the main intersection on my way home from school. They've been talking about putting in a roundabout there for five years, but the city council keeps arguing over the budget. They just spent half a million dollars remodeling the town hall, but they can't fix a single pothole on Main Street. 

So, I don't know... I'm just not sure if it's my face ruining things or if everything is just kind of terrible right now.
Do you think that if someone else watched one of your lesson videos, they would notice the swelling on your face?

Well, yeah... I mean, absolutely they would. I'm actually here because I just... I can't stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face whenever I watch those lesson videos back. It's so obvious. And once I notice it, I just feel like the students, the parents, the staff... everyone must be staring right at it instead of listening to a single word I'm saying. 

Which is a huge problem because half the time the parents aren't listening anyway. You wouldn't believe the emails I get from parents. I had this one mother last week, Mrs. Gable, she sent me a three-page email at 11:30 on a Sunday night demanding to know why her son got a B-minus on his history project. And the thing is, I explicitly outlined the grading rubric on the syllabus at the beginning of the year. I even made them sign a paper saying they read it. But nobody reads anything anymore! It's like society has completely lost the ability to process written information. People just skim headlines on social media and think they're experts. My brother-in-law does that all the time. He'll read one tweet about the economy and suddenly he's lecturing everyone at Thanksgiving dinner about inflation rates. And he sells above-ground pools for a living! He doesn't know anything about macroeconomic theory. But he just talks so loud that everyone eventually just nods and passes the gravy so he'll shut up. 

But yeah... if anyone watched those videos, they would definitely see it. It's all I can see.
Have you ever considered the possibility that the swelling on your face might not be as noticeable to others as it is to you?

Well, no, not really. I mean, how could they not notice? I've told you, I'm here because I just can't stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face every time I have to watch those lesson videos. It's right there. And once I see it, I just know that's all anyone else is looking at. The students, the parents, the staff... they're all just staring at my face instead of listening to a single word I'm teaching them. 

Which, honestly, is incredibly frustrating because I spend hours putting those lessons together. The curriculum we're forced to use this year is an absolute joke. It's this new "inquiry-based" model that some consultant from California sold the district for God knows how much money. It completely skips over the entire Industrial Revolution! How are you supposed to teach American History and just gloss over the Industrial Revolution? It makes no sense. But the district superintendent, Dr. Aris, she's obsessed with these trendy educational fads. She's always going to these expensive conferences in Aspen or wherever, and she comes back with some new acronym we all have to memorize and implement by Monday. Last month it was "SEL"—Social Emotional Learning—which is fine in theory, but she wants us to integrate it into every single lesson. I'm trying to teach the causes of the Civil War, and I'm supposed to pause and ask the kids how they *feel* about the Missouri Compromise. It's absurd. And meanwhile, the actual textbooks are falling apart. Some of them still have George W. Bush listed as the current president. 

But anyway, no. It's obvious. They're definitely looking at the swelling, not listening to me.
Have you ever had someone, like a colleague or a friend, tell you that they don't notice anything unusual about the side of your face that you're concerned about?

No, I haven't... I mean, I don't exactly go around asking them about it. I try to avoid my colleagues as much as possible lately, to be honest. I don't even go into the staff lounge anymore because it's just exhausting. 

Ever since the administration replaced our good Keurig with this cheap, industrial drip machine, the whole room smells like burnt tires by second period. And Janice from the math department is always leaving these passive-aggressive sticky notes on the refrigerator about her almond milk. Like, nobody is stealing your almond milk, Janice! She's just been impossible to deal with ever since the union rep elections last spring. The whole voting process for that was a complete disaster, by the way, because the IT guy was on vacation in Cabo, and the server crashed twice. We had to switch to paper ballots at the last minute, but they ran out of toner in the main office copier. The school won't approve the budget for new toner cartridges unless you fill out three different requisition forms in triplicate. It's like working in the Soviet Union. You spend half your prep period just doing paperwork to get a dry-erase marker. 

So, no, I'm definitely not sitting around the break room asking Janice or anyone else if they notice my face. I just keep to myself, because I know they can see it anyway.
Has anyone ever commented to you about the appearance of your face, either positively or negatively?

No, no one's ever said anything to me about it. Not directly, anyway. But they wouldn't, would they? People are so fake. They'll stare right at you and then pretend everything is perfectly normal. It's just like how nobody says anything about the new bell schedule. 

They changed the passing periods from five minutes to four minutes this semester, which doesn't sound like a big deal, but when you have kids trying to get from the science wing all the way to the portable classrooms out back, it's a nightmare. And the portables are freezing! The heating unit in Portable 3 has been broken since October. I put in a maintenance request, but the district maintenance guy, Gary, is completely useless. He just comes in, looks at the thermostat, sighs, and says he needs to order a part. He's been "ordering a part" for three months. I'm pretty sure he just spends his entire shift sitting in his truck listening to sports radio. I saw him parked behind the cafeteria for two hours last Tuesday when he was supposed to be fixing the leak in the boys' bathroom. It's ridiculous. 

But yeah, no one has actually come up and made a comment about my face to me. They just look.
Have you ever considered that the swelling on your face might not be noticeable to others at all?

I feel like you just... I mean, no. No, I really haven't considered that, because it's just not possible. It's so incredibly obvious. Especially with parent-teacher conferences coming up next week, which is just filling me with absolute dread. 

And of course, the administration decided to schedule conferences right in the middle of the midterm grading window. Which would be bad enough on its own, but they just forced us to switch to this new grading portal, EduTrack, and it is completely broken. It automatically rounds grades down, so I have parents emailing me at eleven o'clock at night complaining that their kid's 89.9 isn't an A. And the district's new policy is that we have to respond to all parent communications within 24 hours, but half the time the school's firewall flags their emails as spam anyway. So I'm sitting there trying to manually override the grades in a system that logs me out every five minutes, and the principal, Mr. Henderson, is sending out these mass emails about our "parent engagement metrics." He actually wants us to start documenting every single phone call we make in this massive, shared Excel spreadsheet that takes ten minutes just to load on my classroom desktop. It's just... it's a total nightmare. 

But anyway, to answer your question, no. I haven't considered that it's not noticeable. I know they can see it. It's all they're going to be staring at during those conferences.
Do you feel like your concerns about the appearance of your face are affecting your relationships with friends or family outside of work?

I don't... I mean, I'm not really sure? I guess I haven't really noticed because I just don't see them much right now anyway. Like, my sister wanted me to come over for my nephew's birthday this past weekend, and I just made up an excuse not to go. 

Plus, driving over to her place in the Heights is a complete nightmare right now anyway because of the construction on I-95. They've had the left two lanes closed for, what, six months? And the detour they set up takes you right through that intersection by the old mall where the traffic lights are completely out of sync. You literally sit there for three full light cycles just to make one left turn. And then when you finally get to her neighborhood, there's zero parking because her HOA has these insane rules where guests can't park on the street, but her driveway only fits two cars. And her husband, Dave, insists on parking his massive Ford F-150 right in the dead center of it. He doesn't even use the truck for work! He's a corporate accountant! He just bought it because he thinks it makes him look outdoorsy, but the only thing he ever hauls is, like, a few bags of mulch from Home Depot twice a year. It's so irritating just dealing with the logistics of going over there. 

So, yeah, I don't really know if my face is affecting my relationships with them. I just stay home.
Do you think it's possible that your concern about the swelling on your face is worse than what others actually see?

I just... no. No, I don't think it's worse than what they see. How could it be? It's right there. It's the first thing anyone would notice. Kind of like how you can't help but notice the smell in the teachers' lounge right now. 

Someone—and I'm pretty sure it's Mrs. Gable from the history department—keeps microwaving leftover fish. Who microwaves fish in a shared space? It's completely inconsiderate. And the worst part is, the ventilation in that room is tied to the main HVAC system, which hasn't been properly serviced since before the pandemic. So the smell doesn't just stay in the lounge, it seeps out into the main hallway right by the main office. You walk past the trophy case and it just hits you. And of course, the school board just voted down the bond measure that would have funded a complete overhaul of the HVAC system. They said it was "too expensive," but then they turned around and approved a brand new turf field for the football team. A turf field! Our textbooks in the science department are literally falling apart—the binding is completely shot on half of them—and they're spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on artificial grass for a team that hasn't won a playoff game in a decade. It's just so backwards. 

But no, I don't think I'm making it worse in my head. I know exactly how bad the swelling is, and I know they can see it just as clearly as I can.
Have you ever considered seeking a medical evaluation to confirm whether the swelling on your face is actually present?

I haven't... I mean, why would I need a doctor to confirm something I can literally see in the mirror every single day? 

But honestly, even if I wanted to go to a doctor, our school district just switched our health insurance to this new HMO plan for the new fiscal year, and it is a complete disaster. They sent out these massive packets right before winter break, expecting everyone to navigate the open enrollment portal which, surprise, crashed on the second day. And if you didn't manually select your primary care physician by the deadline, they just auto-assigned you to someone within a fifty-mile radius. I got assigned to a pediatrician! I'm thirty-two years old and my listed primary care doctor has a waiting room full of toddlers and those giant germ-covered bead mazes. 

I tried calling HR to fix it, but Barbara in benefits retired last month, and the new guy they hired, Kevin, doesn't even know how to check his voicemail yet. I've sent him four emails and he just replies with the same generic PDF attachment that doesn't even open on a Mac. So trying to get any kind of medical appointment right now is just an absolute joke anyway. 

But no, to answer your question, I haven't considered it. I don't need a medical evaluation to tell me my face is swollen. I know what it looks like.
Have you ever taken a picture of yourself and shown it to someone you trust, asking them to tell you honestly if they see any swelling on your face?

I haven't taken any pictures. I mean, why would I want a picture of this? I delete any photos people take of me anyway. 

Although, getting a decent photo right now is almost impossible with the lighting in my apartment. My landlord finally replaced the fixture in the bathroom, but he bought these ridiculously harsh LED bulbs that make the entire room look like a surgical suite. I asked him if we could switch them out for something warmer, maybe like a soft white, but he went on this whole rant about energy efficiency and how much money it saves on the building's overall utility bill. Which is hilarious, considering he still hasn't fixed the drafty windows in the living room. Every time the wind blows from the north, my heating bill spikes by like thirty dollars. I had to buy one of those draft dodgers—you know, the long fabric tubes you shove under the door? I got one shaped like a dachshund off Etsy, which is cute, but it doesn't really solve the problem of the actual window panes rattling in their frames. I've sent him three maintenance requests through that terrible online portal they use, but he just marks them as "resolved" without ever sending anyone out. 

So, no, I haven't shown a picture to anyone. I wouldn't even know who to show it to, honestly.
Do you think it's possible that your concern about the swelling on your face is making it seem worse to you than it actually is?

Worse than it actually is? I... no, I really don't think so. It's not like my mind is playing tricks on me. It's just a fact. It's as obvious as the absolute mess they made of the staff parking lot this week. 

The district finally decided to repave the lot behind the gymnasium, but they hired the lowest bidder, obviously. So they tore up the old asphalt on Monday, and then it rained for three days straight. Now there's this massive crater right next to my assigned spot that fills up like a moat. And the kids in the auto shop class—Mr. Henderson's class—keep driving that beat-up old Honda Civic they're rebuilding right through it to test the suspension. Mud gets everywhere. It splashed all over the side of my Corolla yesterday. I tried to talk to Henderson about it, but he just laughed and mumbled something about "experiential learning." Experiential learning! Meanwhile, I have to keep a spare bottle of Windex in my trunk just so I can see out of my passenger window to safely merge onto the highway to get home. It's ridiculous. The lack of respect for personal property in that building is just staggering sometimes. 

But... what were we saying? Right, my face. No, I'm not exaggerating it in my head. The swelling is exactly as bad as it looks. I'm not making it up.
Do you think it's possible that you're more aware of the swelling on your face than others are?

More aware? I mean... I guess I'm the one who has to look at it the most, especially lately. I'm here because I can't stop seeing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face on the lesson videos. 

Since the district pushed this new hybrid learning initiative, they've been making all the department heads record these sample instructional videos for the junior staff to use. They gave us all these ring lights and tripods, which is a joke because the tripods are so cheap the plastic clasps snap if you tighten them too much. I had to duct tape mine to a stack of American History textbooks just to get it at eye level. And the software they want us to use, Canvas Studio or whatever, it automatically compresses the video file so the audio gets out of sync by like half a second. So not only do I have to stare at myself, but I look like I'm in a badly dubbed foreign movie. I spent three hours on Sunday just trying to re-record a ten-minute lecture on the causes of the Civil War because the audio kept lagging. 

But yeah, once I notice how swollen my face looks on the screen, I just... I can't focus on anything else. I feel like the students, the parents, the other staff members who have to watch these things... they must be staring at it instead of listening to anything I'm saying. How could they not be? It's right there.
Have you considered the possibility that the swelling on your face is not visible to anyone else?

Not visible to anyone else? I... no, I haven't considered that, because it's just impossible. How could they not see it? It's right there. 

Though, I guess sometimes I do wonder what people actually pay attention to. Like my sophomores, for instance. I swear they don't look at a single thing I hand them. I passed back their essays on the Industrial Revolution yesterday, and I had spent my entire weekend leaving detailed feedback. I even used that new rubric the district mandated. Have you seen this thing? It's a four-page matrix with these ridiculous sub-categories like "Syntactic Fluidity" and "Cross-Disciplinary Resonance." I had to sit through a three-hour professional development seminar on Zoom just to learn how to grade with it, and the presenter's microphone kept cutting out because she was using hotel Wi-Fi in Orlando. She was at Disney World for her niece's birthday, which, you know, fine, but maybe don't schedule a mandatory district-wide training when you're literally waiting in line for Space Mountain. 

Anyway, I spent hours on these rubrics, and half the kids just looked at the letter grade on the last page and shoved it into their backpacks. One kid, Tyler, actually left his on the floor under his desk. I found it when I was wiping down the desks after the bell. Just crumpled up next to a crushed juice box. 

But... no, if they can spot a tiny letter grade on the back of a four-page packet, they can definitely see the swelling on my face. It's huge. There's no way they don't see it.
Have you ever considered the possibility that the swelling on your face is not actually there?

Not actually there? I... no. No, of course not. I mean, I can feel it, I can see it. It's not an illusion. It's real. It's as real as that absolute nightmare of a copy machine they just put in the faculty lounge. 

Seriously, they replaced our old workhorse copier over winter break with this "smart" printer, and it has been a complete disaster. It requires a six-digit PIN and a fingerprint scan just to make a black-and-white copy, and half the time the touchscreen doesn't even register your finger. I had to print out 90 copies of a primary source document on the Treaty of Versailles on Tuesday, and the thing jammed on page 42. And of course, Brenda—the main office secretary—was on her lunch break, and she's the only one who has the override key for the toner door. So I'm standing there, trying to pry out a crumpled piece of paper with a paperclip, and Mr. Davis from the math department is standing right behind me, just sighing heavily and tapping his foot because he needs to print his calculus quizzes. He always waits until the absolute last minute. Like, your class starts in four minutes, Davis, maybe plan ahead for once? 

And then when Brenda finally gets back, she treats me like I broke the machine on purpose. She literally pointed to this little wooden sign on her desk that says "Lack of planning on your part does not constitute an emergency on my part." Which is just so incredibly passive-aggressive, considering I was there twenty minutes early. 

But... sorry, what were you asking? If the swelling isn't real? Right. No, I've never thought that. It's definitely there. I wouldn't be sitting in this office if it wasn't. It's huge, and it's ruining my life.

doctor.question: Have you ever considered the possibility that the swelling on your face is not actually there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's insight/delusional belief regarding whether the swelling on his face is actually there or completely imagined (absent). patient.answer:
Not actually there? I... no. No, of course not. I mean, I can feel it, I can see it. It's not an illusion. It's real. It's as real as that absolute nightmare of a copy machine they just put in the faculty lounge. 

Seriously, they replaced our old workhorse copier over winter break with this "smart" printer, and it has been a complete disaster. It requires a six-digit PIN and a fingerprint scan just to make a black-and-white copy, and half the time the touchscreen doesn't even register your finger. I had to print out 90 copies of a primary source document on the Treaty of Versailles on Tuesday, and the thing jammed on page 42. And of course, Brenda—the main office secretary—was on her lunch break, and she's the only one who has the override key for the toner door. So I'm standing there, trying to pry out a crumpled piece of paper with a paperclip, and Mr. Davis from the math department is standing right behind me, just sighing heavily and tapping his foot because he needs to print his calculus quizzes. He always waits until the absolute last minute. Like, your class starts in four minutes, Davis, maybe plan ahead for once? 

And then when Brenda finally gets back, she treats me like I broke the machine on purpose. She literally pointed to this little wooden sign on her desk that says "Lack of planning on your part does not constitute an emergency on my part." Which is just so incredibly passive-aggressive, considering I was there twenty minutes early. 

But... sorry, what were you asking? If the swelling isn't real? Right. No, I've never thought that. It's definitely there. I wouldn't be sitting in this office if it wasn't. It's huge, and it's ruining my life.
